messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Mehta is an eighty-year-old widowed South Asian man who served for decades in the United States Coast Guard and who now presents for his first formal psychological evaluation, referred by his primary care physician following a significant decline in functioning over the past two years. He lives alone in a coastal town in the Pacific Northwest, not far from the station where he spent the final chapter of his career. He is soft-spoken, meticulously dressed, and visibly uncomfortable when asked to speak about why he has come.

The incident that brought Rajan to this point occurred approximately two years ago during a routine training exercise conducted in a heavily forested inlet. He was operating a rigid inflatable vessel in conditions he had navigated hundreds of times before. A younger colleague, a man in his thirties with a family, was working at the bow when Rajan made a navigational correction that he has since replayed without resolution. The vessel struck a partially submerged log, the impact was sudden and violent, and the colleague was thrown against the rail and sustained a severe traumatic brain injury. He survived but has not returned to work and, by all accounts Rajan has gathered, will not. In the immediate aftermath, Rajan stood on the deck of that vessel surrounded by the dense green of the treeline, the cold salt air, the sound of distant emergency sirens growing louder across the water, and he understood, with a clarity he has never been able to fully reconstruct or fully escape, that he had done this.

In the months that followed, Rajan found that his memory of those minutes did not behave as memories should. It did not settle into a coherent story he could examine and set aside. Instead it arrived in pieces — the particular colour of the water, the sound of the impact, the colleague's name being called — disconnected fragments that did not add up to a whole. When he deliberately tried to sit with what had happened, to account for it honestly, the memory seemed to recede from him, as though the mind were withholding something he both needed and could not bear to find. And yet without warning, in the middle of an ordinary afternoon, the scene would return with a completeness that was overwhelming — the smell of the inlet, the cold, the weight of what he had seen — arriving not as recollection but as re-entry.

Rajan has come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that the accident did not happen by chance. He is convinced that something in his character — some fundamental defectiveness he has carried his whole life — was the real cause. He had been reckless before, he tells himself. He had always been the sort of man who acted before he should. When colleagues or family members raise the future — plans, hopes, what the coming years might hold — he grows visibly distressed and changes the subject, as though speaking about the future is a presumption he no longer has the right to make.

He has developed a set of habits that have quietly restructured his daily life. He will not walk in the forested areas near his home, which means he has stopped visiting the trail where he and his late wife used to walk each morning. He enters any room — a waiting room, a restaurant, a community centre — and selects his seat only after surveying the exits and the sightlines. He has begun taking physical risks that are difficult to explain in a man otherwise so careful: driving too fast on unfamiliar roads, declining to wear adequate clothing in cold weather. He avoids unfamiliar places entirely when he can, unwilling to enter any environment he cannot immediately read for danger. When the memory presses too close, he tells himself that it was not really so serious, that perhaps he has exaggerated it all in his mind; he forces his attention toward something neutral or positive; he pushes the images away with a deliberateness that costs him considerably.

What finally brought him in was a phone call from his colleague's wife, who had reached out simply to say there were no hard feelings. Rajan could not speak. He sat with the receiver in his hand for a long time after she had hung up. He is most afraid, he says quietly, that there is no version of himself that deserves to be well.
